text: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.
The tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouth of fools pours out folly.
The eyes of the LORD are everywhere, watching both the evil and the good.
A healing tongue is a tree of life, but a deceitful one crushes the spirit.
A fool despises his father's discipline, but whoever heeds correction gains sense.
In the house of the righteous there is great wealth, but the harvest of the wicked brings ruin.
The lips of the wise scatter knowledge, but the heart of fools holds nothing of the kind.

versions.text: The lips of the wise scatter knowledge, but the heart of fools has none to give.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew simply says "the heart of fools is not so." "Has none to give" adds an idea of giving that is not in the text; a closer rendering keeps the contrast without importing new content while remaining natural for reading aloud.

text: The sacrifice of the wicked is detestable to the LORD, but the prayer of the upright is his delight.
The LORD detests the way of the wicked, but he loves the one who pursues righteousness.
Harsh discipline awaits the one who leaves the path; whoever hates correction will die.
Death and destruction lie open before the LORD—how much more the hearts of men.
A mocker resents being corrected; he will not go to the wise.
A glad heart brightens the face, but a heavy heart leaves the spirit broken.

versions.text: A glad heart brightens the face, but heartache crushes the spirit.
versions.explanation: "Crushes the spirit" duplicates the wording already used for a different Hebrew phrase in verse 4 (שֶׁבֶר בְּרוּחַ). Using "leaves the spirit broken" here keeps the distinct imagery of רוּחַ נְכֵאָה (a stricken/broken spirit) and avoids flattening two proverbs into the same English line.

text: A discerning heart seeks knowledge, but the mouth of fools feeds on folly.
All the days of the afflicted are hard, but a cheerful heart has a continual feast.
Better a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure with turmoil.
Better a meal of vegetables where there is love than a fattened ox with hatred.
A hot-tempered man stirs up conflict, but the patient man calms a quarrel.
The way of the sluggard is like a hedge of thorns, but the path of the upright is a level highway.

versions.text: The way of the sluggard is a hedge of thorns, but the path of the upright is a level highway.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has the comparative prefix כְּ ("like") on מְשֻׂכַת חָדֶק. The translation states an identity rather than a simile; restoring "like" preserves the figure and reads just as smoothly aloud.

text: A wise son brings joy to his father, but a foolish man despises his mother.
Folly is a delight to the senseless, but a man of understanding keeps a straight course.
Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed.
A man finds joy in giving an apt reply—and how good is a word at the right time!
The path of life leads upward for the prudent, keeping him from the grave below.
The LORD tears down the house of the proud, but he sets firm the widow's boundary.
The LORD detests the schemes of the wicked, but gracious words are pure to him.
Whoever grasps at unjust gain brings ruin on his household, but the one who hates bribes will live.
The heart of the righteous weighs its answers, but the mouth of the wicked pours out evil.
The LORD is far from the wicked, but he hears the prayer of the righteous.
A bright look gladdens the heart, and good news gives strength to the bones.
Whoever listens to life-giving correction will be at home among the wise.
Whoever ignores discipline despises himself, but whoever heeds correction gains understanding.
The fear of the LORD is the discipline of wisdom, and humility comes before honor.
